title: sparse-trace-sampling-and-dynamic-correlation-guidelines-2025
author: Maya Chen
content:
Purpose
-------
This document defines Redwood Inference's recommended approach to sparse trace sampling and dynamic correlation of telemetry across services to balance observability fidelity and telemetry cost. It targets tracing for the inference control plane, runtime inference path, and edge gateways. The goal is to ensure we can:

- Maintain high signal for P0 production incidents and performance regression detection.
- Limit trace ingestion cost growth under high request volumes.
- Preserve causal context for aggregated metrics, logs, and traces for troubleshooting.

Scope
-----
Applies to:

- All backend services involved in the request path for inference (API gateway, router, model-serving runtime, autoscaler hooks).
- Sidecars and library instrumentation used by SDKs and internal clients.
- Observability pipelines (OTel collector configs, ingestion filters, storage/retention tiers).

Not in scope: client-side SDKs used by external customers (these follow public SDK guidance).

Principles
----------
1) Signal-first: Ensure full traces are captured for high-value requests (errors, high latency, rollout cohorts).
2) Cost-awareness: Default sampling rates must prevent trace volume from growing linearly with traffic.
3) Dynamic adaptation: Sampling should adapt to traffic patterns and incident state, not be static per-service.
4) Correlation preservation: When a sampled trace exists, correlated logs and metrics must include the trace-id/span-id to aid root cause analysis.
5) Deterministic controls: Policies should be driven by deterministic signals (status codes, latency percentiles, feature flags) and centrally enforced.

Key terms
---------
- Head-sample: Full trace recorded and retained across the pipeline.
- Tail-sample: Lightweight minimal trace (span ids + top-level metadata) stored for statistical analysis.
- Dynamic sampler: A controller that adjusts sampling decisions based on signals (error rate, latency, traffic bursts, manual incident mode).

Sampling strategy
-----------------
1) Default global sampling:
   - Production baseline: 0.5% head-sample rate per service per minute.
   - Tail-sample rate: 5% across the same traffic by default (captures latency distribution without full payloads).

2) Signal-based overrides (always head-sample):
   - HTTP 5xx or internal error codes.
   - Requests with end-to-end latency >= P99 latency SLO * 1.5 for that service.
   - Canary or rollout cohorts marked with the header X-Feature-Cohort: canary (see rollout section).
   - Requests which trigger alerts from the first-line anomaly detector (see rollout steps).

3) Priority paths (higher base sampling):
   - Admin/prod-control-plane operations: 10% head-sample.
   - Model-onboarding and evaluation endpoints: 5% head-sample.

4) Burst protection and throttling:
   - When trace ingestion approaches the budget threshold (default 80% of daily trace quota), the dynamic sampler reduces global head-sample rate by up to 90% in a smooth, exponential backoff over 5 minutes, preserving signal-based overrides.

Dynamic sampling controller design
---------------------------------
- Controller inputs: service-level request rate, error rate, P95/P99 latency windows, current ingestion quota, manual incident mode flag.
- Decision cadence: every 30s evaluate and emit sampling policy deltas.
- Enforcement: policies distributed as flags to OTel SDKs and the gateway sampler via config push.
- Safety: decisions must be reversible and logged to observability so changes are auditable.

Correlation policy
------------------
- All sampled traces (head or tail) MUST propagate the trace-id and span-id as headers: X-Trace-Id and X-Span-Id.
- Services MUST inject trace-id into logs using the platform logger field trace_id and into metrics as a tag trace_id when available.
- When a head-sample exists, logs and heavyweight events for the request are routed to the same retention tier as the trace.

Storage and retention tiers
-------------------------
- Hot traces (head-samples linked to incidents or high-latency events): retained 30 days.
- Warm traces (head-samples not flagged): retained 7 days.
- Tail-samples: retained 90 days at aggregated resolution (no per-span payload).
- Raw span payloads with PII-sensitive fields must be redacted or hashed at the collector before persistent storage (see privacy checklist below).

Operational runbook (incident mode)
----------------------------------
1) Detection: If alerting system raises a cross-service P99 latency or error-rate alert, the oncall engineer runs the Incident Mode command in the observability console.
2) Activation: Incident Mode sets dynamic sampling to: 10% head-sample for all services in the affected product domain, preserves signal-based overrides, and increases logging correlation retention to 30 days for traces related to the incident.
3) Post-incident: Controller automatically decays back to baseline over 2 hours unless explicitly cleared by the incident lead.

Deployment and rollout steps
----------------------------
- Phase 1 (agent rollout): Deploy OTel SDK instrumentation and collector filters to 10% of services (low-risk backend services). Monitor trace volume and latencies for 2 weeks.
- Phase 2 (dynamic sampler enabled): Enable controller in passive mode (only logs decisions) for 1 week. Validate decisions against recorded traces.
- Phase 3 (active sampling): Flip to active sampling in the same 10% cohort. Gradually expand 25% -> 50% -> 100%, verifying budgets and dashboarded ingestion metrics at each step.
- Phase 4 (platform default): Mark policy as default and document per-service overrides in service-level telemetry manifests.

Configuration examples
----------------------
- OTel collector snippet (illustrative):

```yaml
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc: {}
processors:
  batch:
  sampling/dynamic:
    controller_endpoint: https://sampler.internal.redwood/v1/policy
exporters:
  jaeger:
  otlp/http:
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [batch, sampling/dynamic]
      exporters: [jaeger, otlp/http]
```

- Example sampler rule (decision API JSON excerpt):

```json
{ "service": "runtime-gpu-1", "base_rate": 0.005, "tail_rate": 0.05, "overrides": [{"condition": "status >= 500", "rate": 1.0}, {"condition": "header.X-Feature-Cohort == 'canary'", "rate": 1.0}]}
```

Observability dashboards and alerts
----------------------------------
- Required dashboards:
  - Trace ingestion overview (daily/rolling 1h/24h), head vs tail counts, quota usage.
  - Sampling decision heatmap by service and endpoint.
  - Trace-linked latency percentiles with sample-backed histograms.
- Alerts:
  - Trace ingestion > 85% of daily quota -> paging to SRE.
  - Unexpected drop: global head-sample rate change > 50% within 2 minutes (non-incident) -> pager.
  - Correlation gap: % of traces missing trace_id in logs > 1% for 15m -> ticket to owning service.

Privacy and security checklist
------------------------------
- Strip or hash PII fields in span attributes at the collector.
- Only authorized teams may request ad-hoc retention extension for traces; approval captured in ticketing system.
- Sampler control endpoint must require mTLS and use RBAC tied to the deployment pipeline.

Developer guidance and SDK requirements
--------------------------------------
- SDKs MUST support dynamic policy updates delivered via the collector or central config service.
- Instrumentation points: entry API handler, request router, model-inference span, KV/redis cache spans, and db/span for metadata writes.
- Use lightweight spans for cache hits/kv-prefetch and avoid recording large embeddings in span attributes.

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Owners: Observability Platform (primary), Eng Platform (secondary), Serving Runtime (service-level telemetry manifests).
- Oncall: observability-sre rotates the sampler incident pager.
- Escalation path: observability-sre -> eng-platform lead -> runtime-ops -> CTO if cross-domain outage > 4 hours.

Metrics to evaluate success
---------------------------
- Trace coverage for P1 incidents: target >= 95% (head or tail presence).
- Cost per 1M requests traced: target <= $X (tracked in monthly observability cost report).
- Mean time to root cause (MTTR) for latency incidents: target improvement of 20% after rollout.

Appendices
----------
A. Example Grafana queries
  - Head traces per minute: sum(rate(trace_head_count[1m])) by (service)
  - Tail vs head ratio: rate(trace_tail_count[5m]) / rate(trace_head_count[5m])

B. Privacy mapping checklist (quick):
  - Embedding vectors -> never stored in traces.
  - User identifiers -> hashed at collector.
  - Uploaded customer files -> traced only with consent flag.

C. Change log
  - 2024-10-12: Initial draft by Maya Chen.
  - 2024-11-20: Added dynamic controller cadence and burst protection rules (review by Evan Ross).
  - 2025-02-03: Finalized retention tiers and incident mode behavior (review by Priya Narang).

If there are questions about implementation or you need a config review for a service, contact the Observability Platform channel (@observability-platform) and include the service telemetry manifest.
